analysis.one_liner: Overhauls the Clean Air Act: cuts acid rain pollution, tightens smog and car rules, and controls toxic air pollutants.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 25 cosponsors — 21 of 45 Senate Republicans and 4 of 55 Senate Democrats — but after four days of hearings it never received a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act: cutting the sulfur dioxide that causes acid rain by roughly 10 million tons from 1980 levels, sharply reducing smog in the dirtiest cities, regulating toxic air pollutants from factories for the first time in a comprehensive way, tightening tailpipe and fuel standards, and strengthening enforcement with bigger fines and public disclosure of emissions. Power plants, refineries, and automakers would have borne the compliance costs. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which held four days of hearings but never voted it out, and it expired with the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe polluted air: residents of smoggy cities, communities downwind of coal-fired power plants, lakes and forests damaged by acid rain, and people exposed to industrial toxic air pollutants. The bill also required public disclosure of emissions and permit data, gave citizens more enforcement tools, and funded state and local air pollution control agencies. Its sponsor was from Rhode Island, an acid rain–affected state.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smog-city residents and acid rain–affected communities

how_it_helps.text: Cuts acid rain at the source: nationwide sulfur dioxide reductions of approximately 10 million tons from 1980 levels in two phases, plus 2 million tons of nitrogen oxide reductions, aimed at coal-fired power plants.

Creates the first comprehensive toxic air pollutant program: a list of hazardous air pollutants and technology-based emission standards for all major source categories within ten years, with follow-up risk evaluations.

Forces progress in smoggy areas: ozone nonattainment areas are classified by severity with deadlines, and moderate-and-worse areas must cut smog-forming volatile organic compounds by at least 15 percent by the end of 1995.

Cleaner cars and fuels: stricter tailpipe limits on hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen oxides; cold-weather carbon monoxide standards; caps on gasoline vapor pressure; and low-sulfur diesel (0.05 percent by weight) required by October 1993.

Stronger enforcement: administrative penalties, fines and up to 15 years' imprisonment for knowing releases that put people in imminent danger of death or serious injury, rewards of up to $10,000 for tips leading to convictions, and revised citizen-suit provisions.

Public right to know: permits, compliance certifications, and monitoring reports must be available to the public, and the existing exemption that kept emissions records secret as trade secrets is removed.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants would bear the largest costs — meeting the sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cuts through scrubbers or lower-sulfur coal, holding emission allowances, installing continuous monitoring, and paying fees for excess emissions. Oil refiners would have to reformulate gasoline and diesel; automakers would face stricter tailpipe standards and clean-fuel vehicle quotas. Part of these costs would be passed through to electricity ratepayers and drivers.

drawbacks.text: The sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cuts impose major capital costs on coal-burning utilities, and much of that cost would be passed to electricity ratepayers, with the burden falling hardest on coal-dependent regions of the Midwest and on producers of high-sulfur coal.

The bill includes a coal-protection carve-out: state governors could certify compliance plans that bar the use of coal produced outside their state at in-state power plants, which shields local mining jobs but can raise the cost of the required emission reductions.

Fixed clean-fuel vehicle quotas — 500,000 in model year 1995, 750,000 in 1996, and 1,000,000 per year for 1997 through 2004 — lock in specific sales numbers that could cost more per ton of pollution avoided than cheaper measures, although the bill allows the EPA to approve substitutes achieving equivalent reductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gains are broad — less acid rain, less smog, new control of toxic air pollutants, cleaner cars and fuels — and the design includes genuine cost-saving flexibility, such as trading of sulfur dioxide emission allowances and market-based alternative compliance. But the costs are real and unevenly distributed: coal-dependent utilities and their ratepayers, high-sulfur coal producers, refiners, and automakers pay first, and several provisions (out-of-state coal bans, fixed clean-fuel quotas) add cost without adding much protection. On balance the bill trades significant, mostly regional industry costs for nationwide air quality improvements.

outcome.mechanism: It never got a vote: after four days of subcommittee hearings, the Environment and Public Works Committee never reported it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. John Chafee of Rhode Island introduced the bill on August 3, 1989, joined by 24 cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on four days — September 28 and October 3, 4, and 5, 1989.
No committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action followed; the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The regulated industries were better off: with the bill dead, none of its mandates took effect, so coal-burning utilities, high-sulfur coal producers, refiners, and automakers avoided the required upgrades and cuts. People in smoggy and acid-rain-affected regions stayed under the older, weaker rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities and other regulated industries

for.name: Sen. John H. Chafee
for.role: Sponsor, senior member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a 25-member bipartisan cosponsor list from a Republican-led start.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Held four days of subcommittee hearings in September and October 1989 but never reported the bill to the Senate floor.

against.name: Coal-burning electric utilities
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory sulfur dioxide cuts that would force plants off high-sulfur coal, the central fight blocking comprehensive clean air legislation in this period.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred, so the split cannot be measured; the 25 cosponsors were 21 of 45 Senate Republicans but only 4 of 55 Senate Democrats, and the bill died in a committee it never got out of.

industries.note: The bill requires roughly 10 million tons of sulfur dioxide and 2 million tons of nitrogen oxide reductions, permits with compliance plans, continuous emission monitoring, and fees on excess emissions. Their compliance cost is the public's clean-air gain, so their interest runs against ordinary people's here.

Acid rain cuts push utilities toward scrubbers or lower-sulfur western coal, threatening high-sulfur coal sales; the bill partially shields local coal by letting governors certify plans that preclude use of out-of-state coal at in-state plants.

Tighter tailpipe standards, cold-weather carbon monoxide limits, onboard diagnostics, and clean-fuel vehicle quotas rising to 1 million vehicles per year. Cleaner cars are the point; the industry bears the engineering cost.

Gasoline vapor-pressure caps, low-sulfur diesel requirements, vapor recovery at high-volume pumps, and restrictions on nonconforming fuels change refining and blending practices. Fuel changes mean cleaner air for drivers and downwind communities.

industries.industry: Industrial emitters of hazardous air pollutants
industries.note: Title III sets technology-based emission standards for all major source categories of listed hazardous pollutants within ten years. Their cost is communities' reduced toxic exposure.

industries.industry: Pollution-control and clean coal technology firms
industries.note: The bill directs FERC to run an incentive program for clean coal and control technologies, with a federal share of at least 20 percent of qualifying project costs, creating demand for the equipment the bill mandates.
